title: ⭐⭐ Revision: who invented what, and how a word is reversed

questions.prompt: Match each name with the invention your book credits to him.
questions.explanation: Your book credits Willis Carrier with the air conditioner in 1902, which makes it the oldest invention on the list. William Kolff is credited with kidney dialysis in 1944, and dialysis is the machine that does the work of a failing kidney. Gordon Gould is credited with the laser in 1958. Chester F. Carlson is credited with the photocopier in 1937 — and he is easy to confuse with Bell Labs, whom the same answer key credits with the voice recognition machine in 1936, one year earlier. Two other names travel with this list and are worth keeping apart from these four: Berners Lee, who created the internet protocol and HTML in 1990, and James Russel, who invented the compact disk in 1965.

questions.prompt: In three of these words the opening letters are a prefix that reverses the word after them. In the other three the same letters simply belong to the word. Which three carry a reversing prefix?
questions.explanation: incurable is in- plus curable and means not curable. irreversible is the same prefix taking the shape ir- before an r, and it means not reversible. disappear is dis- plus appear and means the opposite of appearing. The other three only look alike: to insert is to put something in, not the opposite of anything; to dismiss is to reject, and it is certainly not the opposite of to miss; to inflame is to make red and swollen, and it is not the opposite of to flame. The test is simple and it never fails you: pull the letters off, and ask whether the word that is left means the opposite of the whole.

questions.prompt: In your module "make-up", "book-case" and "test-tube" are written as one block or joined by a hyphen, while "gene therapy" and "burial services" are written as two separate words. What does the book say this difference does to the pronunciation?

options.text: The one-block words are stressed on their first part; the two-word expressions are not.
The one-block words are stressed on their second part; the two-word expressions are not.
The two kinds are pronounced with exactly the same stress pattern.
The stress falls on the last syllable, whichever kind of expression it is.

questions.explanation: The book's answer to this exercise is that a compound noun written as one block or with a hyphen carries its main stress on the first part, and that the two-word expressions of the section do not behave in the same way — which is exactly why it asks you to say both groups out loud and compare them. "The one-block words are stressed on their second part; the two-word expressions are not." turns that answer round. "The two kinds are pronounced with exactly the same stress pattern." removes the very difference the exercise is built on. "The stress falls on the last syllable, whichever kind of expression it is." invents a single rule for every word in English, and the section exists to show that there is no such rule.

questions.prompt: A pupil begins a sentence about her homework: "I'd rather use a computer ___ ." Which ending finishes the module's structure?

options.text: than to write everything by hand
that I write everything by hand

questions.explanation: When the preference is about your own action, this structure takes two bare verbs on either side of than, which gives "than write everything by hand" after I'd rather use. "than to write everything by hand" adds a to that the second half never carries, since the first half has none either. "than writing everything by hand" puts an -ing form where the bare verb belongs. "that I write everything by hand" replaces than with that and builds a clause; the shape with a subject and a past form is the other one, the one you use for somebody else's action, as in I'd rather you came early.

questions.prompt: Complete this line of a hospital report: "The scanner shortens the time a doctor needs to reach a reliable ___ ." The gap takes the noun built on the verb diagnose.
questions.explanation: The noun English builds on diagnose is "diagnosis", one of the small group in which the noun is not the verb plus an ending, beside choice from choose, proof from prove and suspicion from suspect. "diagnosement" applies a regular ending to a verb that already has its own noun, and the word does not exist. "diagnostic" is an adjective in English — a diagnostic test — and it is the trap for anybody who reads the sentence through French. "diagnosing" is the -ing form of the verb and names the act while it is going on, whereas the gap follows an article and an adjective and needs the thing the doctor arrives at.

questions.prompt: A speaker tells her audience: "Intelligence is not written in one gene. Upbringing, food, school, experience and simple healthy living count as much as the hundreds of genes involved." What is she using this fact to argue?

options.text: That genes have no effect at all on how intelligent a child becomes.
That inserting a gene to raise intelligence is not the simple operation it is sold as.
That schools ought to test the genes of their pupils before admitting them.
That intelligence is far easier to alter by genetic engineering than athletic performance.

questions.explanation: She is answering the promise that a gene could be inserted to enhance intelligence, and her fact undoes it: if hundreds of genes work together and if upbringing, food, school and experience weigh as much as they do, then no single insertion can deliver what is promised. "That genes have no effect at all on how intelligent a child becomes." is refuted by her own sentence, which counts the genes among the factors instead of dismissing them. "That schools ought to test the genes of their pupils before admitting them." builds a policy she never proposes, and it would rest on the very idea she is attacking. "That intelligence is far easier to alter by genetic engineering than athletic performance." separates two things her sentence puts on the same footing.
